t: Tiling a Rectangle with the Fewest Squares — Backtracking Editorial
o: We must cover an n x m rectangle completely with axis-aligned integer-sided squares, using as few squares as possible. For example, a 2x3 rectangle is optimally tiled by one 2x2 square plus two 1x1 squares (3 total), and 5x8 needs 5 squares while 11x13 needs only 6. There is no simple closed-form formula: greedy strategies fail (e.g., always placing the largest square can be suboptimal), so we must search. With n, m <= 13 the search space is small enough for backtracking, provided we fill cells in a canonical order and prune aggressively.
k: Always place the next square at the lowest-leftmost empty cell: this fixes a canonical order and avoids exploring permutations of the same tiling.
Greedy 'largest square first' is NOT optimal (e.g., some rectangles need smaller squares to enable better packing), so we must try every feasible size.
A skyline (per-column height) representation makes finding placement spots O(m) instead of scanning a full grid.
Prune any branch whose current count already reaches the best answer found so far.

a.n: Approach 1: Backtracking on a Boolean Grid
a.i: Scan the grid for the first empty cell (top-to-bottom, left-to-right). Any valid tiling must cover this cell with exactly one square whose top-left corner sits there, so we try every size s from the maximum feasible down to 1, mark the s x s block as used, recurse, then unmark it. The first empty cell anchor guarantees each distinct tiling is explored exactly once regardless of placement order. Prune whenever the current square count reaches the best known answer.
s: If n > m, swap so the grid has at most 13 rows conceptually (symmetry).
Find the first empty cell (i, j); if none exists, update the best answer with the current count.
Compute the largest s such that the s x s block anchored at (i, j) is fully empty and inside the grid.
For s from that maximum down to 1: mark the block, recurse with count + 1, unmark the block.
Return the best count found; initialize best to n*m (all 1x1 tiles).
a.t: Exponential in the worst case, roughly O((n*m)^k) branches where k is the answer, but tiny constants and strong pruning make it fast for n, m <= 13.
a.sp: O(n*m) for the grid plus O(answer) recursion depth.

a.n: Approach 2: Skyline Backtracking with Stronger Pruning
a.i: Instead of a full grid, track only the height of each column (the skyline). The next square must sit on top of the globally lowest column; among ties we take the leftmost one. A square of size s can be placed there only if the next s-1 columns share the same height and adding s stays within n. This shrinks state checks from O(n*m) to O(m) per node and pairs naturally with the count-based prune, giving a large constant-factor speedup.
s: Maintain an array h of length m where h[j] is the number of filled rows in column j.
Find the leftmost column j with minimum height; if that height equals n, the rectangle is complete — record the count as a candidate best.
Compute the largest s such that columns j..j+s-1 all have that same height and height + s <= n.
Try each size s from largest down to 1: raise those s columns by s, recurse, then lower them back.
Prune immediately whenever the current count is >= best.
a.t: Exponential worst case, but each node costs only O(m) and the tighter branching plus pruning makes it comfortably fast for n, m <= 13.
a.sp: O(m) for the skyline array plus O(answer) recursion depth.

w: In an interview, start with Approach 1 to establish correctness (canonical lowest-leftmost anchoring is the key idea to articulate), then upgrade to the skyline version for efficiency. Common pitfalls: assuming greedy largest-square-first works (it does not — e.g., certain rectangles like 11x13 need non-greedy choices); forgetting to try sizes other than the maximum; and off-by-one errors when checking whether an s x s square fits. Edge cases: n == m returns 1, and min(n, m) == 1 returns max(n, m) — both fall out naturally from the search. Likely follow-ups: counting the number of optimal tilings, handling very large n and m (where you would need number-theoretic results or DP over divisors), or tiling with rectangles instead of squares.
